title: Happy Destruction
reviewNotes: Saved montage and captions reviewed, with full native later diagrams checked. Begin after ...Kxb7 at 100 seconds in the complete fifteen-piece later diagram, with White Kf1 and all five white pawns retained. a6+ forces Ka8, and Qd5+ is proved against both Kb8 and Rc6, ending in actual queen mates. The Rc6/Qxc6+/Kb8/Qb7 completion is an explicitly independent line responding to the source’s highlighted blocking resource. The earlier rook and bishop sacrifices, queen capture of Nd7 and alternative sacrifices remain outside this selected proof.
transcript: In chess, there is victory and there is destruction. And the second one is what my friend Happy Chess did in this game. He's playing with the white pieces and yes, he's completely winning having an extra queen compared to the black rook. So here, he decides to start an attack. He pushes the black knight away and now plays queen to E3 pinning the knight to the king. Because of that, black plays now rook H to E8 trying to attack this queen and move it away. But this is the beginning of the end for black because Happy Chess is about to uncork three majestic, brilliant moves starting with rook takes E6 check. A beautiful sacrifice that cannot be accepted because of course, if you take this rook, there is going to be a check with the queen forcing the king to move. Nothing else can be done and on the next move, this would be a checkmate with the bishop and queen battery. So the only other move that black can play is king to B8. Now Happy side steps with the queen playing queen to D6 check. Again, there is only one move for black, king to A8. And now it seems like this is the end of the combination. White is still winning and it's going to win later in the game, right? Well, not exactly. Rook to C8, a brilliant sacrifice that seems to not make any sense. Is the idea to pick up this knight? Surely not. Of course, the sacrifice has to be accepted because this is almost a checkmate. And after this move, Happy follows up with another sacrifice, bishop takes B7 check. Again, the sacrifice has to be accepted. This is the only move. This entire sequence was completely forced. But what's the idea? If we pick up the knight, now black is left with two rooks and this is not even that winning anymore. Did we really sacrifice two pieces for nothing? No, the follow-up is A6 check, a quiet pawn move and there is only one square for the king to move to, B8. And after queen to D5, it doesn't matter that black has all of these pieces. None of them can block the diagonal apart from the rook, but that would be a free piece. Black moves and on the next move, this is an incredible checkmate. If you love incredible chess, follow me for more.
